item.title: (1963) A Christmas Gift for You from Philles Records
item.description: Every track on this album sounds like a cathedral with a dancing congregation.

item.title: (1963) Please Please Me
item.description: Lennon’s vocal on “Twist and Shout” — recorded last, in one pass, because his voice was shredded from ten hours of singing — is raw, elated, riding the edge of physical collapse.

item.title: (1963) Presenting Dionne Warwick
item.description: Most Brill Building records in 1963 moved in 4/4 time and stayed in one key. Burt Bacharach’s songs for Dionne Warwick did neither.

item.title: (1963) The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan
item.description: On all but one of its thirteen tracks, The Freewheelin’ Bob Dylan is a young man, an acoustic guitar, and a harmonica in a neck rack, recorded mostly live to tape in a Manhattan studio across eight sessions and a single year.

item.title: (1964) A Hard Day's Night
item.description: That opening chord — a slashing, harmonically ambiguous voicing musicologists have argued over for decades — announces the album’s central fact: every song here is a Lennon-McCartney original.

item.title: (1964) Another Side of Bob Dylan
item.description: In a single three-hour session on the night of June 9, 1964 — fueled, by one account, by a couple of bottles of Beaujolais — Bob Dylan recorded fourteen new songs, eleven of which became Another Side of Bob Dylan.

item.title: (1964) Presenting the Fabulous Ronettes Featuring Veronica
(1964) The Times They Are a-Changin'
item.description: Every song on The Times They Are a-Changin’ is Bob Dylan’s own, the first of his albums to drop traditional covers entirely, and almost every one is about somebody else’s suffering.

item.title: (1964) Where Did Our Love Go
item.description: The title track opens with foot stomps, handclaps, and a baritone saxophone riff so simple it barely qualifies as a melody, and then Diana Ross’s voice floats in above it, thin and breathy and almost childlike, asking a question the arrangement has already answered by refusing to give her anything ...

item.title: (1965) Bringing It All Back Home
item.description: The first sound on Bringing It All Back Home is a guitar figure lifted almost whole from Chuck Berry, and over it Bob Dylan starts talking faster than anyone in folk music had dared.
